opus-5.5.text:
What stood out most was that his questions went straight to the essence. Many committee members naturally focus on details like the experimental setup, the baselines, and whether the numbers are convincing. Professor Tang didn't spend much time there. He would step back and ask something like, "What problem are you actually solving? If this method works, what does it change about how we understand the problem?"

At the time I was working on generative models, and like many students I was fairly proud of the technical pieces: the architecture designs and the tricks that made training stable. His questions made me realize that those things matter, but they aren't the point. He kept pushing me to explain why the direction was worth doing at all, and where it would lead in five or ten years.

Honestly, I was a bit nervous, because you can't prepare for questions like that by memorizing slides. You have to have thought it through yourself. Looking back, it was one of the most valuable parts of my PhD. It changed how I judge research. Now, when I start a project or advise students, the first thing I ask is whether we can state clearly, in one or two sentences, what fundamental question we're trying to answer. If we can't, no amount of engineering will make the work truly meaningful.

He also had a very calm way of asking. It never felt like he was trying to catch you out. It felt like he genuinely wanted to see how far your thinking went. That attitude of being rigorous but curious left a deep impression on me.

r001.rationale: The response describes questions about the problem being addressed, its significance, and its long-term direction, but does not say Professor Tang asked how the research could be used in practice.

fable-5.1.text:
What stayed with me most was how he went straight past the results and into the "why." I'd prepared a very polished story about the method and the numbers, and he barely touched any of that. Instead he kept asking things like, why does this phenomenon exist in the first place, and what would break if your assumption were wrong. At first I honestly felt a bit exposed, because those weren't questions you could answer by pointing at a table.

But looking back, that was exactly his style. He cared about whether you understood the problem, not whether you could defend a paper. He had this way of asking a very simple question in a very calm tone, and the simplicity was the trap, because a simple question with no clean answer tells you right away where your thinking is shallow. He also pushed on the bigger picture, asking where this line of work would be in five years and whether it mattered beyond the benchmark. That reframing has stayed with me. Ever since, whenever I evaluate a research direction, I hear that voice asking, "but why does this work, and does it matter?"

r001.rationale: The response says Tang asked whether the work mattered beyond the benchmark, but it does not state that he asked how the research could be used in practice.

astra-6.text: What stood out to me was how a simple question could make me reconsider the whole premise of my work. In a defense, you prepare to explain your methods and results, but the harder questions are often: Why does this problem matter? What have you actually understood? That’s the quality of questioning I’d emphasize—the ability to move past the technical details and get to the core of the research.
